claim: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most frequently diagnosed cancer worldwide.
source: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most frequently diagnosed cancer worldwide and the fourth most common cause of death from cancer (Ferlay et al., 2015; Clinton et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferlay et al., 2015 and Clinton et al., 2018

claim: Colorectal cancer is the fourth most common cause of death from cancer.
source: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most frequently diagnosed cancer worldwide and the fourth most common cause of death from cancer (Ferlay et al., 2015; Clinton et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferlay et al., 2015 and Clinton et al., 2018

claim: The genetic component to risk of colorectal cancer is thought to explain up to 35% of variability in CRC risk.
source: There is a genetic component to risk of the disease, which is thought to explain up to 35% of variability in CRC risk (Huyghe et al., 2019; Czene et al., 2002; Lichtenstein et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huyghe et al., 2019; Czene et al., 2002; Lichtenstein et al., 2000

claim: Obesity is thought to increase CRC risk.
source: In addition, modifiable lifestyle factors, including obesity, consumption of processed meat, and alcohol, are thought to increase CRC risk (Clinton et al., 2018; Händel et al., 2020; McNabb et al., 2020; Lauby-Secretan et al., 2016; Gui et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clinton et al., 2018; Händel et al., 2020; McNabb et al., 2020; Lauby-Secretan et al., 2016; Gui et al., 2023

claim: Consumption of processed meat is thought to increase CRC risk.
source: In addition, modifiable lifestyle factors, including obesity, consumption of processed meat, and alcohol, are thought to increase CRC risk (Clinton et al., 2018; Händel et al., 2020; McNabb et al., 2020; Lauby-Secretan et al., 2016; Gui et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clinton et al., 2018; Händel et al., 2020; McNabb et al., 2020; Lauby-Secretan et al., 2016; Gui et al., 2023

claim: Alcohol consumption is thought to increase CRC risk.
source: In addition, modifiable lifestyle factors, including obesity, consumption of processed meat, and alcohol, are thought to increase CRC risk (Clinton et al., 2018; Händel et al., 2020; McNabb et al., 2020; Lauby-Secretan et al., 2016; Gui et al., 2023).

claim: Early-stage CRC or precancerous lesions are largely treatable.
source: While CRC has higher mortality rates when diagnosed at later stages, early-stage CRC or precancerous lesions are largely treatable, meaning CRC screening programmes have the potential to be highly effective (Meester et al., 2020; Cardoso et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meester et al., 2020; Cardoso et al., 2021

claim: CRC screening programmes have the potential to be highly effective.
source: While CRC has higher mortality rates when diagnosed at later stages, early-stage CRC or precancerous lesions are largely treatable, meaning CRC screening programmes have the potential to be highly effective (Meester et al., 2020; Cardoso et al., 2021).

claim: Both systemic and intracellular tumour metabolism play an important role in CRC development and progression.

claim: Several major risk factors for CRC are known to have profound effects on metabolism.

claim: Obesity has been shown via conventional observational and Mendelian randomization analyses to strongly alter circulating metabolite levels.

claim: Mendelian randomization uses genetic variation as a proxy measure for traits in an instrumental variable framework to assess the causal relevance of the traits in disease development.

evidence: This is a description of the MR method based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Germline genetic variants are theoretically randomized between generations and fixed at conception.
source: As germline genetic variants are theoretically randomized between generations and fixed at conception, this approach should be less prone to bias and confounding than conventional analyses undertaken in an observational context.

claim: The ALSPAC cohort recruited 14,541 pregnant women with an expected delivery date between 1 April 1991 and 31 December 1992 from the former Avon County of southwest England.
source: ALSPAC is a population-based birth cohort study in which 14,541 pregnant women with an expected delivery date between 1 April 1991 and 31 December 1992 were recruited from the former Avon County of southwest England (Boyd et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boyd et al., 2013

claim: 13,988 ALSPAC offspring alive at 1 year have been followed repeatedly with questionnaire- and clinic-based assessments.

claim: All instrument sets from the reverse MR analysis had an F-statistic greater than 10.

claim: There was little evidence of an association of CRC liability on any of the circulating metabolites investigated in the reverse MR analysis based on FDR-P < 0.05.
source: There was little evidence of an association of CRC liability (overall or by anatomical site) on any of the circulating metabolites investigated, including when the SNP in the FADS gene region was excluded, based on our pre-determined cut-off of FDR-P < 0.05; however, the direction of effect estimates was largely consistent with those seen in ALSPAC GRS analyses, with higher CRC liability weakly associated with higher non-HDLs, lipoproteins, and fatty acid levels (Supplementary file 1f and g).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study results

claim: A previous MR analysis suggested an effect of increased BMI on several measures of circulating cholesterol.
source: One possible explanation for how circulating levels of total cholesterol, VLDL-cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B could predict (without necessarily causing) future CRC development could be linked to diet. A previous MR analysis suggested an effect of increased BMI on several measures of circulating cholesterol (Gui et al., 2023).

claim: Consuming a diet which is high in fat may increase CRC risk both through and possibly independently of adiposity, alongside increasing levels of circulating cholesterol.

claim: The median age at diagnosis of CRC is 64 years.
source: Given that the participants in the ALSPAC cohort are many decades younger than the average age of diagnosis for CRC (mean age 25 y in the latest repeated measure analysed in ALSPAC; whereas the median age at diagnosis of CRC is 64 y) (Granados-Romero et al., 2017), the former seems the most likely scenario.
evidence: Supported by citation to Granados-Romero et al., 2017
